summary:
Deep Space Mission Commander is an interactive game that lets students design, fund, launch and manage a space mission. Players choose a target (Moon, Mars or Asteroid), a rocket, a power source, an antenna and science instruments, all within a $1000M budget and the limits of rocket weight and power supply. The spacecraft then flies across the screen in five phases, and emergencies such as solar flares and micrometeoroid hits force the player to choose between safe and risky responses. The mission ends with a one-to-three-star rating based on the science returned and the budget left over.

The game teaches students how to balance cost against performance, respect mass and power limits, plan data links, and make decisions under uncertainty. It runs in any browser as a single HTML file.
details:
What it does
This is a space mission game where you build your own spacecraft and send it into space. You choose where to go, which rocket to use, how to power it, and what instruments to bring, all on a limited budget. Then you watch it fly, and when emergencies hit, you decide what to do. At the end, you get a star rating.

Why it matters
Real space missions involve tough choices, but students rarely get to try them. This game lets you feel those trade-offs yourself. You learn that you can’t have everything, and that a good plan means balancing cost, weight, power, and risk.

Who it’s for
Anyone curious about space, especially students who want to learn engineering in a fun way. It works in any web browser, so there’s nothing to install.

How we built it
We made the game with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using a canvas to draw the spacecraft’s flight. It’s hosted online with GitHub Pages, and our presentation was made in PowerPoint and saved as a PDF.

What we tried to get right
We wanted the game to be easy to start, so anyone can play it right away. We also tuned the difficulty so a simple Moon mission feels doable, while Mars and asteroid missions challenge you to plan better.
